records.text: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS on BIOLOGY and BIOMEDICINE Angel Canelo, Ines Tejado, Jose Emilio Traver, Cristina Nuevo, Blas M. Vinagre A Human-inspired Simulator for the Study of Orientation and Balance Control A� NGEL CANELO, INE� S TEJADO, JOSE� EMILIO TRAVER, CRISTINA NUEVO, JAVIER PRIETO-ARRANZ School of Industrial Engineering BLAS M. VINAGRE University of Castilla-La Mancha Industrial Engineering School Avenida Camilo Jose� Cela, s/n 13071 Ciudad Real University of Extremadura SPAIN Avenida de Elvas, s/n 06006 Badajoz Javier.PrietoArranz@uclm.es SPAIN {itejbal,jetraverb,bvinagre}@unex.es Abstract: Biologically, the vestibular feedback is indispensable to the ability of balancing for both humans and humanoid robots in different conditions. This paper presents a human-inspired orientation and balance control of a three degree-of-freedom (DOF) simulator that emulates a person sitting in a platform. In accordance with the role in humans, the control is essentially based on the vestibular system (VS), which regulates and stabilizes gaze during head motion, through modeling the behavior of the semicircular canals and otoliths in the presence of stimuli, i.e., linear and angular accelerations/velocities derived by the turns experienced by the robot head on the three Cartesian axes. The semicircular canal is used as the angular velocity sensor to perform the postural control of the robot. Simulation results in the MATLAB/Simulink environment are given to show that the orientation of the head in space (roll, pitch and yaw) can be successfully controlled by a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) with noise filter for each DOF. Key�Words: Vestibular system, Model, Robot, Simulation, MATLAB. 1 Introduction Human balancing ability requires both visual and vestibular feedback. To this respect, there has been a considerable progress over the last years to identify, understand, and model the underlying mechanisms of human postural control, especially for applications in robotics [9, 16]. In humans, the vestibular system (VS), along with other sensory and motor systems, is responsible for three cognitive functions that support mobility: it helps humans to maintain the balance of the body, to stabilize the head, and, when the body or head is in motion, to maintain the visual gaze on a target. Hence, the VS runs as a sensor of the angular motions (more precisely, by means of the semicircular canals) and translational motions (thanks to the otoliths), so that the human body can use all the information collected by such a system to maintain balance, perceive the environment and control its position. These functions show the great importance of the VS for human life. Bearing these human skills in mind, the robotics community is currently progressing towards developing objective standards, among which defining benchmarks that allow objective comparisons [9]. Likewise, advances in such skills may also help to the progress of, for example, robotic rehabilitation devices. The work presented in this paper is a first step towards the former of the mentioned applications. The design of a biologically-inspired artificial VS as a sensor for controlling robot heads during motion has received a great interest in robotics to regulate and stabilize gaze. Complete models of eye-head stabilization based in human skills have been addressed in e.g. [5, 7, 8, 12, 19, 20, 21]; most of them include the model validation on humanoid robots. These are just a few examples of the investigations that can be found in the literature. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the balanc

Complete models of eye-head stabilization based in human skills have been addressed in e.g. [5, 7, 8, 12, 19, 20, 21]; most of them include the model validation on humanoid robots. These are just a few examples of the investigations that can be found in the literature. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the balance of robots that are not endowed with a vestibular sensor is clearly inferior that of humans [10]. The objective of this work is to design and develop a balance control based on the human VS of a three degree-of-freedom (DOF) robot that emulates a person sitting in a platform or chair. More precisely, position of the head (or gaze) of the robot has to be controlled during its motion. For that purpose, a model of the robot will be developed in the MAT- E-ISSN: 2224-2902 10 Volume 16, 2019 WSEAS TRANSACTIONS on BIOLOGY and BIOMEDICINE LAB/Simulink environment. The robot head will include a model of the VS, which will be essentially constituted by the semicircular canals and otolithic organs. The orientation of the head in space (roll, pitch and yaw) will be controlled by a proportionalintegral-derivative (PID) controller, using the semicircular canal as angular velocity sensor. There is thus a double motivation for this research. The principal motivation is to emulate human balancing ability on a 3-DOF robot from a model of the human VS. The second motivation is to show that classical PID controllers can perform successfully the orientation of the robot head using vestibular feedback from the semicircular canals. For simulations, the stimulation of the VS will be carried out to observe the behaviour of the semicircular canals and otoliths as follows: semicircular canals will be stimulated by the angular velocities obtained from the kinematic model of the robot, whereas otoliths (otolithic macula) will be stimulated by linear accelerations. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarizes the human VS from both physiological and mathematical points of view. Section 3 is devoted to the simulator of the 3-DOF robot that has been developed to study orientation and balance control. Section 4 contains the simulation results obtained when controlling the robot with classical PID controllers. Conclusions and future applications are drawn in Section 5. 2 Human Vestibular System This section describes the human VS from both physiological and mathematical points of view. 2.1 Physiological background The VS is a cuboid cavity located in the inner ear, specifically in the center of the bony labyrinth. It is formed by the vestibule and the semicircular canals. Inside the vestibule there are two membranous structures [3]: the utricle and the saccule. In these structures, there are peripheral receptor organs, called macules (Figure 1(a)), which are composed of sensory ciliated receptor cells covered by a horizontal membrane on which there is a series of calcium carbonate crystals. These crystals, called otoliths, are very susceptible to linear accelerations or decelerations in the three planes of space because of the density difference between the otoliths and the macula. In each inner ear the two otolithic receptor regions in the utricle and the saccule are approximately orthogonal to one another, allowing almost any direction of linear acceleration stimulus to be transduced. In what concerns the semicircular canals, there are tree, one horizontal and two vertical [3]. They are cylindrical tubes that form two thirds of a circumference and are oriented in the three planes of space, so that the plane of each of them forms with the other two a 90 angle (Figure 1(b)). The semicircular canals are filled with a pristine fluid called endolymph. The stimulation factor of the semicircular canals are angular accelerations, either by rotation of the head or rotation of the whole body. Likewise, the semicircular canals lead into the vestibule at their two extremes, one of which, called ampulla, has a double diameter, whereas the other is where the recipients of rotations, the ampular crests, reside. These crests are covered by a gelatinous substance rich in mucopolysaccharides, called cupula. 2.2 Mathematical modeling Next, we are going to focus on the mathematical models of semicircular canals and otoliths, which are the essential components of the VS. 2.2.1 Semicircular canals Angular motion sensation relies on inertial forces, caused by head accelerations, to generate endolymph E-ISSN: 2224-2902 11 Volume 16, 2019 WSEAS TRANSACTIONS on BIOLOGY and BIOMEDICINE Table 1: Parameters of the semicircular canal model [13]. The components of the angular acceleration vector resulting from this subsystem, either expressed in the system R0 (consideration of orthogonal semicircular canals) or in the system R3 (consideration of non-orthogonal semicircular canals), are integrated to obtain the angular Figure 5: Appearance of the 3-DOF robot in Simulink. velocity vector and, subsequently, each component of this vector is introduced into the transfer function (2). As a result, the volume of the endolymph displaced by the cupula in the three semicircular canals (posterior, anterior and lateral) is obtained. � The linear acceleration vector that will be introduced in the otolith transfer function (3) is obtained by the subsystem Utricle & saccule. The connection between the two main blocks is due to stimulation of the VS: the outputs of both the kinematic model of the robot and the utricle and saccule, namely, angular and linear accelerations, respectively, are the inputs to the dynamic model of the VS. This model, in turn, is composed by the model of semicircular canals, which will be stimulated by the angular velocities, and the one corresponding to otoliths (otolithic macula), which will be stimulated by the linear accelerations. It should be remarked that it is possible to choose if the person also experiences a translation motion. In this case, another vector of linear acceleration will be added to the linear acceleration vector obtained from the angular motion (the one that has been calculated in the subsystem Kinematics). 3.2.2 Postural control The robot is on a rotating platform and in turn can make three turns emulating the turns of the head (roll, pitch and yaw). For this purpose, the robot has two joints and, in turn, the head allows the relative rotation with the part where it is held. Furthermore, if we now consider that the head ex- periences different rotations in the different axes at the instants t = 10 s and t = 25 s, the displaced volumes in the semicircular canals are shown in Figure 11 for the orthogonal and non-orthogonal cases. For the former (Figure 11(a)), it can be stated that each semicircular canal is stimulated with the component of the angular acceleration vector that corresponds to its respective orthogonal axis (anterior with the component Y ; posterior with the component X; lateral with component Z). In addition, the lateral canal first suffers volume displacement due to the angular acceleration produced by the chair in the head, and then that of the turn over the Z-axis (yaw) of the robot head at instants t = 10 s and t = 25 s. In the case of non-orthogonal canals, as can be observed from Figure 11(b), a volume displacement is produced in the three canals with the rotating motion of the chair, which is obviously greater in the lateral canal. However, at the rotation instants, the anterior and posterior canals begin to experience a larger volume displacement that is obviously caused by the component of the angular acceleration vector of the head that coincides with the orthogonal axis of the respective semicircular canal. But for the second scenario, a lower stationary error is obtained, as well as lower overshoot (see Figure 13(b)). 5 Conclusion This paper has presented the balance and orientation control of a three degree-of-freedom (DOF) simulator that emulates a person sitting in a platform based on the human vestibular system (VS) to regulate and stabilize gaze during head motion. The VS was essentially modeled through the behavior of the semicircular canals and otoliths in the presence of stimuli, i.e., linear and angular accelerations/velocities derived by the turns experienced by the robot head on the three Cartesian axes. The semicircular canal was used as the angular velocity sensor to perform the postural control of the robot. We have developed a neuromorphic convolutional neural network (CNN), FlyVisNet, that is based on the fly's visual system architecture. FlyVisNet implements neural pathways that allow pattern recognition, enabling the detection of objects in different shapes and looming objects. We found that FlyVisNet outperformed other architectures of the same size segment in the classification accuracy of objects of different complexities. With its small size, it allows to be deployed in the most memory and power demanding embedded systems such as nano drones. FlyVisNet allowed visually guided navigation and collision avoidance of virtual and real agents. vii The fly encodes these visual inputs into visual reflexive behaviors. For that purpose, the different neural pathways need to be coordinated when they share a motor actuator such as the fly's wing muscles. In visual reflexive behaviors, it has been found that the fly uses an internal signal, the efference copy (EC), to suppress self-generated visual optic flow. This mechanism allows the fly to stabilize its flights and prioritize specific visual inputs. We provide an integrative model for reflexive visual behaviors in which an EC mechanism permits to coordinate fly's different pathways in complex visual environment with multiple visual patterns. We found that our virtual fly responded faster to the visual patterns when using EC. We also found behavioral evidence of EC when the flying fly navigates in cluttered visual environments. In goal-driven behaviors, the fly can find specific places via visual cues. Through a preliminary study, we have built a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework in which an autoencoder (AE) maps the visual inputs into a fly's central brain-like latent representation. By using FlyVisNet as encoder, an agent could navigate to find a target in a virtual environment. Overall, we have demonstrated that Drosophila's brain can be used as a baseline to develop vision-based navigation algorithms. Our algorithms outperformed other architectures of similar size and allowed artificial agents to perform visually guided navigation in complex visual environments. Our results highlight the importance of brain-inspired computations for a deeper understanding of their biological counterparts, with potential applicability to other domains. viii Chapter 1. Introduction Organisms perceive the external world through a multitude of sensory mechanisms, each finely tuned to detect specific stimuli. These stimuli can range from light and sound to touch, taste, and smell. The process of perception involves the reception of these stimuli by sensory organs, their transmission to the brain, and the interpretation of these signals to form a coherent representation of the surrounding environment. Once the sensory perception of the external world is integrated organisms generate behavior. For example, a plant might grow towards a source of light, a predator might stalk its prey using visual and olfactory cues, or a human might withdraw their hand from a hot surface upon sensing pain. These behaviors are crucial for survival and reproduction, as they enable organisms to respond appropriately to environmental stimuli, avoid danger, and seek out resources. Likewise other reverse engineering examples in history such as the Soviet Tupolev Tu-4 based on the American B-29 bomber or the space rocket Explorer 1 based on the German V-2 rocket that provided such good results, mimicking these biological processes i

Likewise other reverse engineering examples in history such as the Soviet Tupolev Tu-4 based on the American B-29 bomber or the space rocket Explorer 1 based on the German V-2 rocket that provided such good results, mimicking these biological processes in artificial systems can lead to more adaptive and intelligent behavior for machines. By incorporating sensory perception-like mathematical models, artificial agents can interact more effectively with their environment and perform tasks with greater autonomy and versatility. Sensory perception in artificial agents is possible through the use of sensors that detect various environmental stimuli. For example, cameras can capture visual information, microphones can record sound, and pressure sensors can detect touch. These sensors provide data similarly to biological counterparts and by analyzing them provide insights about the surroundings. Once sensory information is obtained, artificial systems can employ brain1 inspired algorithms to process and interpret this data and produce intelligent decision-making. Such is the case of artificial neural networks (ANNs) that can be trained to recognize patterns in sensory input and make predictions or decisions based on this information. For instance, a self-driving car can use visual input from cameras to detect obstacles and make decisions about steering and braking. Among all modalities of sensory, vision surpasses them in its ability to provide rich, multidimensional data about the environment, offering insights into spatial relationships, object recognition, and temporal dynamics. Implementing vision-based algorithms inspired by biological counterparts for artificial agents would allow processing information and produce versatile behavior for a wide range of tasks. This would improve agents' autonomy and adaptability in dynamic and complex environments. 1.1 Motivation and basic approaches Reverse engineering the human brain is an endeavor that sits at the pinnacle of scientific ambition and curiosity. However, the brain's complexity is staggering, with its billions of neurons interconnected in intricate networks, orchestrating human thought, emotion, and behavior. Attempts to mimic the brain's neural processing led to the birth of artificial intelligence (AI). Despite significant advancements in neuroscience, understanding the brain in its entirety remains elusive. In light of these challenges, scientists have turned to simpler organisms to unravel the mysteries of neural circuitry. One such organism is the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, renowned for its relatively simple yet function- 2 ally sophisticated brain. While vastly different from the human brain in scale and complexity, the fruit fly brain has been studied extensively and dissected at a cell level with the recently released connectomes [1, 2]. This makes the fly a perfect baseline and opportunity to develop new AI. Specifically, its visual system of about 80,000 neurons allows it to navigate, either flying or walking, through complex environments with stunning precision. Their ability to process visual information in real-time, often with limited computational resources, is a prove of the efficiency of evolutionary design. In the present thesis, the fly's visual system is used as a baseline to develop ANNs and flight control algorithms that are used as the "brain" of artificial flying agents, both virtual and real. In the present thesis, the fly's visual system is used as a baseline to develop ANNs and flight control algorithms that are used as the "brain" of artificial flying agents, both virtual and real. We derive algorithms from quantitative experimental analysis as well as mathematical modeling that allows the agents to fly in cluttered environments performing visual reflexive behaviors and collision avoidance. The Drosophila visual system involves compound eyes with numerous ommatidia, each housing photoreceptor neurons (PRs) [3]. Among its visual remarkable features, motion detection [4] is facilitated by specialized neurons such as the lobula plate tangential cells (LPTCs) and the horizontal system (HS) cells [5]. These neurons enable the fly to perceive moving objects, optic flow, etc. allowing a quick response to changes in its visual environment. Pattern recognition is another key function of its visual system. Through the integration of signals from multiple ommatidia and subsequent processing in the deeper layers such as the Lobula and optic glomeruli [6], Drosophila is capable of perceiving shapes and patterns in their surroundings [7, 8]. Particularly, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), inspired by the structure of the visual cortex in animals, are exceptionally adept at learn- 3 ing hierarchical representations of images. This hierarchical approach enables them to capture intricate patterns and features at different levels of abstraction, from edges and textures to complex objects and scenes. CNNs have demonstrated unparalleled performance across various visual recognition tasks. Through layers of convolutional, pooling, and activation operations [9], CNNs can efficiently extract and process visual information, making them exceptionally powerful tools for computer vision tasks. CNNs can be trained by using supervised learning, which permits the network to learn from labeled examples, where each input image is associated with a corresponding label or class. During the training process, the network adjusts its parameters iteratively to minimize the distance between its predictions and the ground truth labels, typically measured using a loss function. This training is often accomplished using gradient-based techniques like backpropagation, where gradients of the loss function with respect to the network parameters are computed and used to update the weights. Thus, the intrinsic characteristics of CNNs make them a perfect approach to build a comprehensive model of the visual system of Drosophila. Previous studies have shown that CNNs can be applied for such purpose in collision detection tasks [10, 11], classification [12], and optic flow detection [13, 14], but they mainly implemented partial circuits or early to medium visual layers. In this thesis, we have built the FlyVisNet, a CNN that includes neurons from the retina to deep higher visual centers such as lobula and optic glomeruli, that extract high-level visual features. We show that the artificial neurons' responses are in line with the real ones and that embedded in artificial agents allows visually guided navigation. Once the fly extracts and processes the visual features, it will generate visual reflexive behaviors. Once the fly extracts and processes the visual features, it will generate visual reflexive behaviors. These behaviors represent the interplay between 4 sensory input and motor output and are adaptive strategies employed by flies to navigate their environment effectively. Among these behaviors are the optomotor response, bar fixation, and spot aversion. The optomotor response is a reflexive behavior observed in flies where they adjust their body orientation in response to visual motion. When exposed to a rotating visual stimulus, such as stripes or bars moving in a specific direction, flies will reflexively orient themselves to maintain their position relative to the moving pattern [15, 16, 17]. Bar fixation is another visual reflexive behavior observed in flies, where they fixate on and follow a narrow, elongated visual stimulus, such as a dark bar or stripe [18, 19]. This behavior is thought to aid in maintaining stability during flight and may also play a role in visual navigation. Spot aversion refers to the avoidance behavior exhibited by flies when they tend to move away from short object like spots, possibly as a mechanism to avoid potential threats or disturbances [20, 19]. Dynamical systems theory presents a mathematical approach for capturing the temporal evolution of these behaviors, considering how visual sensory stimuli and internal states dynamically interact to produce observable motorrelated actions. Particularly, control theory techniques allow to implement feedback mechanisms and design control strategies to regulate the fly's behavior in response to environmental stimuli. Previous works have shown dynamical system models of the fly for visuomotor behaviors in which visual input generated gaze angle of the fly [17, 21]. A similar approach was used to model proprioceptive-based feedback control [22]. In these studies, only one single input was provided at a time. In this thesis, we provide an integrative dynamical system model of the visuomotor reflexive behaviors of the fly for complex visual environments where multiple visual patterns take place simultaneously. 5 We have implemented an efference copy (EC) mechanism to coordinate different visual pathways that can activate a common actuator, the wing muscles. EC is a copy of motor-related signals that suppress self-generated visual stimulus [23], allowing the fly to suppress undesired visual inputs [24, 25, 26]. Besides the visual reflexive behaviors, the processed visual features can also be encoded into internal representations for goal-driven behaviors such as spatial navigation. There exist neural pathways that connect the visual system with the central complex's ellipsoid body projection gall (EPG) neurons [27]. By using this pathway the fly can associate visual cues with reward in a navigation-based visual learning task [28]. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a convenient approach to model such behaviors in the fly. The reward prediction error signal central to RL algorithms bears similarities to dopamine-mediated reinforcement signals observed in the brain of flies and other animals. Specifically, the central complex is involved in processing and integrating visual information to create a representation of the surrounding space [29, 30]. This representation forms the basis for the internal model used in model-based RL. Agents would use its internal model to plan sequences of actions that lead to desired outcomes [31]. This unparalleled capability has long fascinated scientists and philosophers alike. What makes the brain truly remarkable is its efficiency. Despite its vast complexity, the brain operates on about 20 watts of power, roughly equivalent to a dim light bulb. With this efficiency, the brain integrates sensory inputs, learns from experience, and solves complex problems in real-time. AI began trying to unlock the secrets of the brain's intelligence and cognition. One of its early steps was when Norbert Wiener introduced the term "cybernetics" in the 1940s [37], which laid foundational concepts for understanding feedback systems and their application to intelligent machines. He explored how all intelligent behavior was the result of feedback mechanisms and how that could be applied to create self-regulating systems and machines that can learn from their environment. Another important milestone was the introduction of neural networks, computational models designed to mimic the brain's neural architecture. The McCulloch-Pitts neural model, developed by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943, simplified the biological neuron (see Figure 1.2 A, B) into a mathematical abstraction, showcasing how neurons could be computationally modeled [38]. Their model was based on the idea of binary threshold logic, where neurons either "fire" (output a signal) or remain inactive based on the weighted sum of their inputs. In the 1950s, Frank Rosenblatt introduced perceptrons (see Figure 1.2 C), early prototypes of neural networks capable of learning from input data through weighted connections [39]. Specifically, they identified distinct types of neurons in the visual cortex with specific receptive fields--areas of the visual field that trigger neural responses. They classified neurons into "simple cells" and "complex cells." Simple cells responded to oriented edges and lines within specific positions and orientations, while complex cells showed less positional specificity but responded to oriented stimuli over larger areas. A pivotal observation was the hierarchical organization of neurons in the visual cortex. They found that simple cells in the primary visual cortex project to complex cells in higher visual areas, indicating a pathway for 10 progressively complex feature extraction and processing of visual information. Their research not only elucidated fundamental principles of visual pro- cessing but also inspired advancements in the understanding of cognition and the development of posterior neural networks. This is the case of Fukushima's Neocognitron in 1980, a pioneering convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture aimed at emulating visual processing and feature extraction in the brain [42]. The progress continued by delving deeper into the brain's workings, developing algorithms like backpropagation in the 1970s [43, 44]. This algorithm allowed not a single perceptron but a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to efficiently learn from training data, adjusting the strengths of connections between artificial neurons, mirroring the brain's synaptic plasticity. It was the introduction of LeNet-5 in the 1990s [9], that made artificial neural networks (ANNs), especially CNNs, as we know them nowadays. This was one of the earliest successful applications of CNNs, demonstrating the effectiveness of convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers in a systematic architecture (see Figure 1.3). This work laid the groundwork for deeper CNNs by showing how to hierarchically extract features from images. Furthermore, researchers found that increasing the depth of CNNs (i.e., stacking more convolutional and pooling layers) enabled better representation learning and hierarchical feature extraction. Thus, Alexnet [45] propelled CNNs into the spotlight, showcasing their capability in large-scale image classification tasks. Recently, brain-inspired models have continued improving performance in different tasks. This is the exciting case of a vector-based navigation agent using grid cells-like representation that outperformed existing models [46], the 11 Figure 1.3: A diagram of a representative CNN architecture. SlowFast model for video recognition based on the visual ventral/dorsal stream [47], and the c. elegans-based neural network policy for autonomous driving [48]. 1.3.2 Drosophila's vision Regarding the previous successful cases of brain-inspired AI, one model organism well established in neuroscience is the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. This insect offers an opportunity as a platform to develop new AI algorithms because its brain while being simpler than the mammalian brain still presents all the basic functionalities. Fly's brain has been dissected at a cell level via the connectomes released recently [1, 2] providing connectivity detail such as synaptic counts, synaptic neurotransmitter polarities, etc. Particularly, the optic lobe of about 80,000 neurons can perform multiple functions simultaneously through different neural circuits, such as motion detection, pattern recognition, looming detection, spatial navigation, etc. [49]. Fly's visual system has a columnar layer-based structure performing visual processing of different complexity upon deeper layers [5]. Electrical signals originating from photons are transduced through the rhabdomeres [50] within 12 the retina layer. This information then progresses through various layers of the visual system. Initially, it flows towards the early layers such as lamina and medulla, and subsequently to deeper layers including lobula and lobula plate [5] (see Figure 1.4 A). The optic glomeruli, a higher-order visual center, plays a crucial role in complex feature detection [6] (see Figure 1.4 A). The visual system follows a retinotopic structure where the visual surround is projected retinotopically onto the dendrites of subsequent neurons [3] (see Figure 1.4 B). The resolution of about 800 ommatidia at the retina layer is maintained through the layers up to the output of lobula/lobula plate cells where there is a biological pooling to about 40 resolution [1] (see Figure 1.4 B). The visual system also encompasses distinct ON and OFF pathways, dedicated to detecting moving bright and dark edges respectively [51, 52, 53, 54]. These pathways ultimately converge onto motion-detecting neurons T4 and T5 [55, 56], enabling motion direction selectivity [4]. Deeper within the layers, specific neurons like LC11 and LC15, with dendrites in lobula and axons projecting to optic glomeruli, exhibit specialized responses. LC11 responds to small objects such as spots, while LC15 detects long objects like bars [7, 8]. The intricate connections upstream to these neurons and higher centers have also been meticulously mapped [57]. In the lobula, another crucial neuron, LPLC2, functions as a selective looming detector [58]. Complementing this function, an adjacent neuron, LC4, encodes the velocity of approaching objects [59]. Upon the recognition of the visual features of the scenery the fly will generate visual-reflexive behaviors. The visual centers process the visual input and the motor centers will activate the corresponding wing muscles to generate the proper reflexive behavior (see Figure 1.5 A). In the case of complex visual 13 environments, multiple visual features are processed in different visuomotor circuits that can trigger a shared actuator, such as the wing motor system. A theory of how to manage this coordination is an EC mechanism. This theory posits that during movement, the nervous system generates a copy of the motor command, which is then compared with sensory feedback to predict the consequences of the movement. Essentially, it helps animals distinguish selfgenerated sensory signals from externally generated ones [23]. In such cases the behavior of the fly is modulated not only by external visual input but also by an internal state [60] (see Figure 1.5 A). One of these reflexive behaviors is the optomotor response which is the ability to track and respond to visual motion patterns, particularly the opt

In such cases the behavior of the fly is modulated not only by external visual input but also by an internal state [60] (see Figure 1.5 A). One of these reflexive behaviors is the optomotor response which is the ability to track and respond to visual motion patterns, particularly the optic flow, which is the perceived motion of objects as the observer moves through the environment. When a fly is in motion, the visual world around it shifts accordingly. For instance, as it flies forward, objects in its field of view move backward. Once the optic flow is detected and analyzed, the fly's motor system is activated to generate appropriate behavioral responses. This typically involves adjusting the orientation and position of the fly's body and wings to counteract any deviations from its intended trajectory [15, 16, 17] in response to horizontal or vertical gratings. For example, if the optic flow suggests that the fly is veering to the left, it will adjust its wing movements to steer back to the right, effectively stabilizing its flight path (see Figure 1.5 B). Another intriguing aspect of its behavioral repertoire is the bar fixation behavior. This behavior involves the fly's ability to fixate on and track a moving visual stimulus, such as a narrow bar or stripe, within its visual field. Bar fixation serves various purposes, including navigation and object tracking. When presented with a moving bar or stripe in their environment, Drosophila 14 exhibits a characteristic response wherein they actively orient themselves to keep the bar within their field of view [18, 61, 19] (see Figure 1.5 B). This behavior is observed both in tethered flies and in free-flying individuals in more naturalistic environments [20]. Contrary to the previous, spot aversion behavior in Drosophila refers to their instinctive response to avoid spots in their environment. When Drosophila encounters spots or short small objects, they typically exhibit a series of avoidance maneuvers [20, 19] (see Figure 1.5 B). These can include changes in locomotion, such as rapid turns or retreats, as well as alterations in wing posture. One proposed explanation for spot aversion behavior is that flies have evolved to associate dark spots with potential dangers, such as predators or obstacles. In nature, dark spots could indicate hiding places for predators or areas of reduced visibility where collisions with objects are more likely. By avoiding these areas, flies can increase their chances of survival. Recent studies in Drosophila have proven the existence of EC signals in an array of visual neurons during both spontaneous and visually evoked rapid flight turns [24, 25, 26]. Thus, in cluttered visual environments when the fly may encounter gratings in the background and long stripes in the foreground EC can mediate to generate proper behavior (see Figure 1.5 B). 1.3.3 Fly vision models Models of fly vision have been established to mimic its visual processing. Furthermore, dynamical system models using feedback control have shown the utility of fly vision for flight control [65, 17, 21]. Models using the Hassenstein-Reichardt motion detector allowed robots to navigate avoiding collisions [66, 67]. ANNs have been also used to model fly vision. Partial implementations have provided solutions in collision detection tasks [10, 11], and classification [12]. Also, connectome-based ANNs implementing early visual layers achieved direction selectivity-like responses [13, 14], providing a deeper understanding of neural processing that complements the connectome data and solving tasks such as optic flow detection. 1.3.4 Vision-based artificial agents fly vision-inspired models are expected to be more power and memory efficient than those mimicking larger visual systems, so it might be useful in applications with memory and power limitations, such as drones. Particularly, fly vision models might be ideal for controlling small drones. In fact, there is a trend in shifting the technology and application of drones, transitioning from radio-controlled models to advanced systems driven by AI. This evolution has transformed drones from simple remote-controlled gadgets into sophisticated aerial platforms capable of autonomous decision-making and complex tasks [68, 69]. AI algorithms allow them to interpret and understand their surroundings in real-time, enabling autonomous flight and decision-making. AI-driven drones excel in object recognition and tracking. They can identify and track objects of interest such as vehicles, people, animals, or specific landmarks [68, 70]. Also, AI-driven drones employ advanced obstacle detection 18 and avoidance techniques based on vision. They can dynamically detect and navigate around obstacles in their path, ensuring safe and efficient flight even in complex environments [71]. Among drones, nano-sized drones present the most demanding memory and power constraints, becoming necessary to design optimized AI algorithms. In this direction, the introduction of AI microcontroller units (MCU) has permitted to run CNN models on an ultra-low power basis. These microcontrollers require networks of small size architectures and low memory. Well-established architectures for classification such as ResNet [72] need to be adapted for these types of controllers. Thus, the DroNet, based on ResNet, was embedded successfully in an AI processor optimized to execute CNNs, which was assembled on a low-power nano drone, and proved to be effective for steering control and collision avoidance [73]. FlyVisNet: an insect vision-inspired artificial neural network for the control of a nano drone 2.1 Summary Flying insects exhibit remarkable visual computation capabilities despite having a limited number of neurons. Specifically, the fruit fly Drosophila's visual system consists of 110, 000 neurons, and its neural circuits have been steadily dissected at the level of single cells. Among them, visual projection neurons have been found to sense different features such as a looming visual object, optic flow, and objects in specific shapes. In this work, we have developed a neuromorphic Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), FlyVisNet, in which we have implemented the visual projection neurons LC11, LC15, and LPLC2 as well as all their upstream connections including T4/T5 motiondetecting neurons from the ON/OFF pathways. We compared its accuracy on a classification task to other vanilla CNN architectures of a similar scale. We found that FlyVisNet achieved higher accuracy for two different datasets than the other CNNs, even with a reduced number of parameters, thereby requiring less memory. Furthermore, the artificial neurons of our network, after being trained for the classification, reproduced selectivies of real neurons, in terms of the shape and direction of visual pattern. Finally, we tested FlyVisNet embedded in a nano drone, in virtual as well as in real environments. With an onboard ultra-low-power parallel processor dedicated to FlyVisNet, the drone achieved high performance in terms of the response time and memory requirement. Our results highlight the importance of brain-inspired computations 20 for a deeper understanding of their biological counterparts, as well as for the application to other domains, particularly in embedded systems with memory and power limitations. 2.2 Introduction The brain's neural processing has long inspired artificial intelligence, ranging from artificial neuron models to perceptrons and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [38, 39, 42]. In particular, neocognitron, the first CNN, was developed based on the study of orientation-selective feature-detecting neurons in the cat's visual cortex [40, 41]. The convolution operation in this network was designed after the visual property of so-called simple cells in the visual cortex, which can be obtained by adding visual tuning of presynaptic neurons. Although the resulting CNN architecture has been foundational for recent progress in artificial intelligence, attempts to build an artificial neural network mimicking a more detailed organization of a visual system have been scarce. With the advent of the full brain connectome in Drosophila, alongside premiere genetic toolkits, behavioral and physiological experimental assays, it has become possible to dissect the structure and function of single visual neurons in depth [1, 2]. Among 200, 000 neurons in the Drosophila brain, more than half were shown to be involved directly in visual processing [75, 76], making it one of the most visual organisms. The system consists of five early visual structures: retina, lamina, medulla, lobula, and lobula plate. Vis

Among 200, 000 neurons in the Drosophila brain, more than half were shown to be involved directly in visual processing [75, 76], making it one of the most visual organisms. The system consists of five early visual structures: retina, lamina, medulla, lobula, and lobula plate. Visual processing in these structures consists of columnar structures corresponding to each compound eye lens, detecting various local visual features while main- 21 taining the spatial dimensionality. When these structures pass local visual feature signals to central brain regions, the feature information converges from a large visual field to a singular structure, which exhibits responses to different visual patterns such as translating spots and bars or approaching objects [7, 8, 57, 58, 59]. These structures represent a concise visual system for visual feature detection, making it an ideal target for brain-inspired artificial neural networks. The Drosophila visual system has been previously used for building visual feature detection systems [62, 66, 14, 13]. For example, the HassensteinReichardt motion detector model based on dynamical systems where a differential activation of photoreceptors with a temporal delay served as a foundational concept for understanding how flies detect and respond to visual motion [62]. Further improvements of this model allowed robots to navigate without collisions [67]. Simulations of a part of the visual system have been reported through ANNs [14, 13, 12, 10], providing a deeper understanding that complements the connectome data and solving tasks such as image classification, optic flow detection, and collision avoidance. These implementations could be useful in applications with memory and power limitations such as drones. Since the fly brain-inspired models are expected to be more energy efficient than those after a larger visual system, they might be useful for applications requiring less energy, such as a drone. Moreover, there has been a significant shift in the technology and application of drones, transitioning from radiocontrolled models to advanced systems driven by ANNs [68, 69]. One key aspect of ANN-driven drones is their autonomy, allowing them to make decisions based on the data collected from their surroundings. They can navigate complex environments, avoid obstacles, and even collaborate with other drones 22 to achieve specific objectives [68, 70, 71]. Among such applications, nano-sized drones present one of the most challenging platforms to operate ANN-based algorithms because of their memory and power limitations. Alongside the development of ANN-compatible microcontrollers, Drosophila brain-inspired neural network may be adequate for nano-sized drones [73, 74]. In this study, we present the implementation of a neuromorphic CNN inspired by the structure of the Drosophila visual system. We named this network FlyVisNet and designed it to mimic the neural circuits crucial for detecting translating or approaching visual objects. FlyVisNet incorporates artificial neurons representing visual neurons transmitting visual feature information to the central brain, along with early visual neurons essential for computing these features. When trained to detect simple visual features, FlyVisNet demonstrated superior accuracy compared to the existing lightweight network, such as MobileNetV2, despite having a comparable network size. Among these VPNs, three cell types known for their high visual selectivity are LC11, LC15, and LPLC2 (see Figure 2.1 A). LC11 neurons get activated in response to the movement of a small object, regardless of the movement direction [7]. LC15 neurons depolarize selectively to the horizontal motion of a vertical stripe, again regardless of the direction [8]. Finally, LPLC2 cells respond to both an approaching object and a translating small object [58, 59]. We built a model around these three types of VPNs to sense translating or approaching visual objects. Each neuron is implemented as a convolution layer with a main building block of convolution operation followed by activation and max-pooling (see Figure 2.1 B and see Figure 2.S1) (see Methods 2.5.1). We present 2 versions, the fly version following the retinotopic 800 ommatidia resolution [3] of input images and the drone version for its camera resolution of 244x324 (see Figure 2.1 B). In the fly version, the max-pooling is only applied in the last layer (see Figure 2.S1). The convolution kernels are initialized with positive or negative uniform values depending on whether their real counterpart is excitatory or inhibitory, respectively. These values are constrained to maintain the polarity during optimization. To implement a visual feature detection network centered around these three VPN types, we incorporated their presynaptic visual circuits into the model. To implement a visual feature detection network centered around these three VPN types, we incorporated their presynaptic visual circuits into the model. LC11 cells receive their primary excitatory inputs from T2/T3 neurons, columnar neurons projecting from the medulla to the lobula [7]. LC15 cells receive the majority of their inputs mainly from TmY4 and TmY9 [8, 77]. To enhance its feature selectivity, we also added inhibitory interneurons that were hypothesized in a previous study [8], corresponding to 25 Li27 identified in a connectome [1] (see Figure 2.1 A, B). Finally, LPLC2 cells respond to a looming object pattern with the majority of their inputs from T4, T5, LPi, and Tm5f [58, 59, 77] (see Figure 2.1 A). T4/T5 neurons are the first to show direction selectivity to bright/dark moving edges respectively in a direction-dependent manner [4, 55, 56]. One recent study showed that LPLC2 neurons form their feature selectivity by integrating visual inputs from both the lobula and the lobula plate [78]. In the lobula, they receive the majority of inputs from trans-medullar neurons such as Tm5f. In the lobula plate, the majority of excitatory inputs come from T4/T5 neurons, which are well known for their direction-dependent motion response to local edges. LPLC2 neurons also receive inputs from inhibitory neurons, such as LPi11 neurons, to enhance their direction sensitivity [78]. To endow T4/T5 neurons with their direction-dependent motion sensitivity, we incorporated all the major medulla neurons presynaptic to these neurons, such as Mi1, Tm3, Mi4, Tm9, Tm1, Tm2, Tm4 cells. We implemented a processing delay to some of these medulla neurons (see Figure 2.1 B) by shifting the input batch one frame. Peripheral to medulla neurons, we incorporated all the R1-R6 neurons in the retina and L1-L3 neurons in the lamina. LC neurons at the final stage of FlyVisNet are implemented as convolution layers with a relu activation function (see Figure 2.1 B and see Figure 2.S1). The LC neurons project their axons into the optic glomeruli and from there they connect with neurons in the central brain. We concatenated the outputs of LCs and through one hidden fully connected layer for 3 output classes (see Figure 2.1 B and see Figure 2.S1). records.text: 2 Classification performance of FlyVisNet To train our network to classify images through feedforward visual pro- cessing, We made a moving pattern dataset that presents visual features for Drosophila. We generated images in sequences of 25 frames featuring mov- ing bars and spots of random width. We also included sequences of looming squares expanding from random positions (see Figure 2.2 A). The brightness of the background and the objects is generated randomly. We also added a uniform random noise component of 5% to each pixel for a better training generalization of natural conditions. For the loom squares, we applied loom label. For moving bars and spots, we used bar and spot labels respectively (see Figure 2.2 A). We generated a set of 7500/750 training/testing frames of 27 244x324 size (drone camera resolution), and another set of 20x40 size, aiming to emulate the fly's 800 ommatidia resolution [3]. For an additional comparison, we chose the COIL-100 dataset [79], which we resized to the previous resolutions. This dataset contains images of 100 different objects filmed on a rotating table and captured from different angles (see Figure 2.S2 A). The objects have different complexity, being some of them natural-based like fruits and vegetables, which could be familiar to the actual fly, whereas others are more artificial like cars and cans that could be challenging to classify. Since our network was to be embedded in the drone, we checked how well our network could do on the classification task of these datasets in comparison to the other networks of similar size designed for embedding applications. We divided the datasets into batches for the training loop and optimized on accuracy (see Methods 2.5.2). For the accuracy performance comparison, we chose Dronet [73] and MobileNetV2 [80], architectures with a similar range of parameters. We varied the hyperparameter to maintain MobileNetV2 size similar to FlyVisNet's. We found that after training on the pattern dataset of resolution 20x40, FlyVisNet achieved a 92.80% test top accuracy, 2.57% higher than MobileNetV2 (see Figure 2.2 B and Table 2.1). To achieve this accuracy FlyVisNet used 78,226 parameters and 1200KB, which is slightly less than MobileNetV2. Additionally, when we initialized the convolution filter weights as random uniform instead of maintaining the synaptic polarity initialization, the accuracy dropped by 1% (see Figure 2.2 C and Table 2.1). These results suggest that our architecture is light and powerful enough to classify simple patterns in a similar way as the fly can do. For a resolution of 244x324, FlyVisNet achieved a 98.53% test top accuracy, slightly higher than Dronet and 2.07% higher than MobileNetV2 (see 28 Figure 2.2 D and Table 2.1). To achieve this accuracy FlyVisNet used 116,626 parameters and 1660KB, which is significantly less memory than Dronet and slightly less than MobileNetV2. Additionally, when we initialized the convolution filter weights as random uniform instead of maintaining the synaptic polarity initialization, the accuracy dropped by 3% (see Figure 2.2 E and Table 2.1). When training on COIL-100 dataset of resolution 20x40, FlyVisNet obtained 99.14%, which was slightly higher accuracy than in the pattern dataset (Table 2.1). This is most likely due to the absence of uniform noise in this dataset as well as the empty background of the frames. Our architecture could classify successfully the objects of different complexities with 6.65% higher accuracy than MobileNetV2 (see Figure 2.S2 B and Table 2.1), and also higher than the randomly init

In a further test, we checked how variations in the architecture would affect the network performance on the pattern classification. We performed a selective pruning of different convolution layers and a general pruning of 80% sparsity. For the resolution of frames 20x40, by removing the R16 convolution layer the top accuracy dropped by 0.80% (Table 2.S1). The network needed similar training epochs to converge to the top accuracy (see Figure 2.S4 A). When we removed T4 and T5 layers the accuracy dropped by about 3% which proved the importance of these layers (see Figure 2.S4 A and Table 2.S1). By applying a pruning of 80% sparsity, the accuracy dropped significantly by about 10% still reducing a significant amount of non-relevant parameters and memory (Table 2.S1). In the case of resolution 244x324, the accuracy drop rates were similar to the lower resolution case (Table 2.S1). Since FlyVisNet follows the fly's visual system architecture, we were specially interested in targeting the motion direction and feature-detecting neurons T4, T5, LC11, LC15, and LPLC2 (see Figure 2.3 A). To obtain the 1D activation, that is the response over time, we passed to the network a visual stimulus through a sequence of frames. Then, we captured the 2D activations, that is the output of each activation function after the convolution, and computed the mean over all the neurons that made up the layer to obtain the averaged 1D response (see Figure 2.3 B). The polarity constraints on the kernels ensured their polarity during training (see Figure 2.S5), so the feature maps from the main inputs to T4/T5 maintained the polarity predominance for a moving bar (see Figure 2.S6). When targeting T4/T5 neurons, we presented to the network a bright moving bar in a preferred direction (PD), that is from left to right, and in a non-preferred direction (ND) (see Figure 2.3 C). We found that the 1D activation response of T4 showed greater amplitude to the PD bright edge of the moving bar, as previously reported for the biological counterpart [55] (see Figure 2.3 C). In the case of T5 response, which detects dark moving edges, it also showed greater amplitude for PD dark edge of the moving bar as has been reported [56] (see Figure 2.3 C). We found that the oscillations in these responses were due to the max pooling operation. We targeted the same neurons for the 20x40 fly version without the pooling and indeed did not exhibit any oscillations (see Figure 2.S7 A). Nonetheless, we have used as main architecture the drone ver- 31 sion with pooling given the benefits in accuracy performance. We also checked the response of the original FlyVisNet before being trained. The motion direction selectivity still worked but not as well as with the training (see Figure 2.3 D). When the convolution kernels were randomly initialized we found a loss in selectivity in T5 or even inversion in T4 (see Figure 2.3 E). We also measured the 2D activations averaged over time that showed the preference for the PD (see Figure 2.S8 A). So the artificial neurons T4, and T5 trained exclusively for a classification task, exhibited direction selectivity in line with those of the fly. When targeting LC11 and LC15, we showed to the network a moving bar and a moving spot. For the moving bar case, LC15 showed a greater amplitude response than LC11 (see Figure 2.3 F) as it was found in the fly [8]. The fly version of the network did not produce oscillations (see Figure 2.S7 B). The 2D activations also showed this preference (see Figure 2.S8 B). For the moving spot, LC11 response was greater than LC15's (see Figure 2.3 G) as reported previously for the fly [7]. The non pooling version neither showed oscillations (see Figure 2.S7 C). The 2D activations additionally demonstrated this selectivity (see Figure 2.S8 C). Therefore LC11 and LC15 showed feature selectivity. For the LPLC2 case, we presented to the network a looming spot and compared LPLC2 to LC15 responses. LPLC2 showed greater amplitude response showing looming selectivity (see Figure 2.3 H) as it was found previously [58, 59]. The 2D activations complemented these results (see Figure 2.S8 D). Once the network had been trained, we designed a virtual 3D world environment to test an artificial agent that runs FlyVisNet on board (see Figure 2.4 A). We prepared an arena layout for a visually guided flight test that had three attached patterns on its walls, a square, a rectangle, and a circle (see Figure 2.4 A) (see Methods 2.5.3). To perform the flight test we retrained FlyVisNet by including as label the X centroid coordinate of the objects to be trained through regression. We designed a flight algorithm that provides commands to the drone depending on the detected class by the network. In this algorithm, the expected sequence is to fly straight while using the predicted X coordinate to keep the object in the center of the field of view (see Figure 2.4 B). When the object is too close will be detected as loom and the drone will turn to the left if the previously detected class is spot. It will turn to the right if the previously detected class is bar. If a loom is detected and the number of detections is reached it will land (see Figure 2.4 B). Once we had tested FlyVisNet with the virtual agent, we repeated the process with the nano drone. We followed an end-to-end process to deploy the network on the drone and perform an autonomous flight. We chose Bitcraze's crazyflie 2.11 drone (equipped with an STM32 processor), which includes as an accessory an AI-based electronic module, the AI deck 1.12. This module is equipped with a camera and a GAP83 processor, which allows to execute embedded CNNs. To control the drone during flight we tested two strategies, a server-based and an onboard AI-based strategy. In the server-based strat- egy, the AI deck module sends the captured frames to a computer via WiFi where the network runs the inference. Depending on the inference results dif- ferent motor commands are sent via radio from the computer (by using the 1. https://www.bitcraze.io/products/crazyflie-2-1/ 2. https://www.bitcraze.io/products/ai-deck/ 3. https://greenwaves-technologies.com/gap8_mcu_ai/ 41 crazyradio PA 2.4 GHz USB dongle) to the crazyflie drone (see Figure 2.5 A). For the onboard AI-based strategy (see Methods 2.5.4), we quantized the trained network on a virtual machine platform to a fixed 8-bit resolution and developed a control flight algorithm application code. We flashed the network application code in the memory of the GAP8 processor and the flight control algorithm in the STM32 (see Figure 2.5 B). In this strategy, the AI deck module captures the image, the GAP8 runs the inference using the quantized version of FlyVisNet, and the result is sent to the crazyflie via UART. Depending on the inference result specific motor commands are directly computed in the drone's STM32 (see Figure 2.5 B). In the GAP8, we set an internal clock frequency of 250MHz for the Fabric Control (FC) and 175MHz for the Cluster (CL). We compared both strategies in terms of cycle time, that is the time needed between capturing a frame and executing a motor command. As a reference, we also compared the cycle time with respect to MovileNetV2. The onboard strategy showed faster cycle time than the server-based, being FlyVisNet faster than MovileNetV2 in both strategies (see Figure 2.5 C). In the server-based approach, the cycle time was about 195ms for FlyVisNet, around 40ms for the inference, and 155ms for communications and executing control commands. The difference with respect to the MobileNetV2's inference was just about 5ms (see Figure 2.5 C). Given that the inference was performed in the computer's GPU, this difference was significantly small. The cycle time of FlyVisNet in the onboard setting was near 150ms in total. The network inference took about 99ms and the UART transmission along with the flight control algorithm execution about 51ms. The difference with respect to the MobileNetV2 inference was approximately 16ms (see Figure 2.5 C). The significant cycle time difference between both strategies h

To perform a flight test with the drone, we built two high-contrast arenas by mimicking the virtual environments that we created previously (see Methods 2.5.5). We performed the drone flight via the on-board strategy. In the layout for the 3 patterns-based flight (see Figure 2.5 D), for 12 trials we placed the drone in the same initial position. Similarly to the simulated agent, the drone took off and approached the spot (square), when loom was detected turned left, flew towards the bar, and upon detection turned right. It landed when loom was detected while approaching to the spot (circle) (see Figure 2.5 E, and Movie 2.S4). The position density map showed that the trajectory was consistently within the same area (see Figure 2.5 F), validating the FlyVisNet utility for a visually guided flight. In the second layout (see Figure 2.5 G) for 11 trials we placed the drone again in the same initial position. The drone took off, flew towards the bar until loom was detected, then turned 180 degrees, flew towards the opposite bar until loom was detected, and turned away again repeating this loop several times (see Figure 2.5 H, and Movie 2.S5). The mean trace showed a displacement in the y-axis, which was due to the fact that when turning 180 degrees away from the bar, the wind generated by the rotors pushed the drone laterally for being close enough to the walls (see Figure 2.5 H). The position density map showed that the drone was consistently in the center of the arena (see Figure 2.5 I). This test proved that FlyVisNet allowed the drone to reproduce the Buridan's paradigm [81] as in the case of the virtual agent. 43 2.4 Discussion The utility of mimicking the Drosophila's visual system for artificial neural networks has been highlighted, as reported in the case of a classification task of conspecifics through a reduced part of the visual system [12]. Through the release of the recent connectomes [1, 2], the implementations can be put into cell level. This was shown in a study where a hexagonal connectome-based neural network also captured the direction selectivity of T4/T5 neurons and the spatiotemporal receptive field of many of the neurons of the visual system [14]. However, there has not been a suitable applicability in the use of artificial agents or autonomous systems which have power and memory limitations. In fact, insect vision-inspired algorithms have been applied in robotics for flight control or navigation tasks based on optic flow detection of the fly via elementary motion detectors [66, 67, 82]. Also, an implementation of a looming detecting neuron algorithm from the locust allowed collision avoidance of a mobile robot [83, 84]. Specifically, Drosophila's LPLC2 neuron mechanism for looming detection has been implemented in silico showing its potential utility [10, 11, 85]. Still, these implementations were focus

records.text: optic flow detection of the fly via elementary motion detectors [66, 67, 82]. Also, an implementation of a looming detecting neuron algorithm from the locust allowed collision avoidance of a mobile robot [83, 84]. Specifically, Drosophila's LPLC2 neuron mechanism for looming detection has been implemented in silico showing its potential utility [10, 11, 85]. Still, these implementations were focused on a specific neural pathway for a specific function that allowed collision avoidance tasks. In this work, we have implemented different neural visual pathways that perform different functions simultaneously. We have not only implemented the ON/OFF pathways that end up in T4/T5 neurons but also the deeper LC neurons in the Lobula layer that can identify objects of different shapes. We have discovered that the neurons of our artificial neural network while being trained exclusively for classification, naturally exhibited emergence of direction selectivity to moving objects in T4/T5. It also emerged selectivity to small objects 44 in LC11 and long objects in LC15 as well as LPLC2 exhibited selectivity to expanding objects. This resulted in a capital characteristic that permitted to perform a visually-guided flight of a virtual agent as well as a nano drone. Our network also showed higher accuracy in classification tasks of simple and complex objects while being memory efficient. It also allowed to control the nano drone within a faster cycle time than the representative embedded-oriented architecture MobileNetV2. The onboard AI-based strategy demonstrated faster flight control of the drone without additional external communications. Furthermore, our embedding level achieved here provides an alternative approach to other extensively used and power-demanding hardware such as Raspberry Pi. In fact, the GAP8 processor at a maximum internal clock frequency of 250MHz for the FC consumes 10mW4 along with 175MHz for the CL can consume a total power of about 100mW [74], whereas a basic Pi model such as Raspberry Pi 2 B consumes 2.3W5. Therefore, we provided a fully autonomous flight-controlled drone that can operate remotely at very low power and memory. However, our system has shown to be highly sensitive to changes in the luminance level, making sometimes wrong pattern recognitions in brighter spaces. In addition, fast maneuvers should be also avoided, because the captured image should be stable to allow a proper recognition. Crazyflie equipped with the AI deck showed to consume the drone battery quite fast, which led to short autonomous flight time. The drone is small enough to be also sensitive to weak gusts of wind, which led to a loss of stability. 4. https://greenwaves-technologies.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Product-BriefGAP8-V1_9.pdf 5. https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html#typicalpower-requirements 45 Given the pros and cons of our flight system, it could be useful in applications with power and size constraints, such as monitoring and management of areas of difficult access, or those areas dangerous for people due to pollution, toxicity, etc. Additionally, it could be also applied in surveillance tasks, and as a remote security system. Still, FlyVisNet has a partial portion of neural circuits implemented, which opens new future lines of work to expand the design by including additional functionalities associated with the visual system of Drosophila. In the first place, we quantized the FlyVisNet TensorFlow Lite model to a fixed 8-bit, which consists of reducing the resolution of the network parameters from 32 to 8 bits. This allows to reduce the used memory, and it is a necessary step for embedding in microcontroller units (MCU), such as the GAP 8 processor. To do so, we used the GAPflow tools provided by GreenWaves Technologies, which are included in the virtual machine. Through this process, we obtained the quantized CNN model into header C files, which can be included in the application code that was flashed and run in the AI deck's GAP8 unit. In the second place, we included the algorithm for autonomous flight in the application code that was flashed and run in the crazyflie's STM32 unit. Both units are connected via UART and run each respective application code simultaneously. 2.5.5 Building an environment for the drone In the case of the environment for the drone, we mimicked the virtual one and built two high-contrast arenas one for the 3 patterns-based and the other for a Buridan's paradigm flight of 60x90 cm. A visual EC-based navigation algorithm in Drosophila for complex visual environments 3.1 Summary Drosophila visuomotor processing has been intensively studied in recent years, leading to a detailed understanding of individual neural circuits. However, the collective operation of these circuits during naturalistic behaviors, in which flies encounter a mixture of complex visual stimuli--including those caused by their own actions--remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed an integrative model of Drosophila visuomotor processing, wherein multiple visuomotor circuits interconnect through an efference copy (EC) mechanism. We first derived simple visuomotor models by analyzing wing responses to individual, rotating visual patterns. We then combined these models to predict wing responses to the superposition of the visual patterns, using three different strategies. We then combined these models to predict wing responses to the superposition of the visual patterns, using three different strategies. We compared orientation behaviors of these models with those of flying Drosophila that rotates their body freely in complex visual environments. The results of these experiments supported one of the EC-based models, in which the amplitude of the flight turn is unaffected by the background scene, irrespective of the visual environment. Together, our "virtual fly" model provides a formal description of vision-based navigation strategies of Drosophila in complex visual environments and offers a novel framework for assessing the role of constituent visuomotor neural circuits in real-world contexts. 63 3.2 Introduction Fruit flies demonstrate impressive agility in flight [88, 89, 90, 91], and vision plays a pivotal role in flight control, often translating directly into precise flight maneuvers. Neural circuit mechanisms underlying many of these visuomotor behaviors have been studied intensively in recent years, both structurally and functionally [92, 93, 94, 51, 95, 96, 49]. While we have gained a qualitative grasp of the neural substrates underlying various visual behaviors, a quantitative understanding remains less explored [59, 4, 97, 8]. In the pioneering era of insect vision in the 1950s to the 1970s, research heavily leaned towards computational modeling. For instance, the ReichardtHassenstein elementary motion detector was formulated to explain visual locomotion behaviors observed in beetles [62]. Another example is the model of EC (EC) that was put forward to describe the visual behavior of hoverflies [98, 23]. While some recent studies have offered quantitative models for Drosophila visual circuits [99, 100, 55, 101], most focused on circuit mechanisms for visual feature detection, without considering its behavioral context. To contextualize the function of these circuits within behavior, a phenomenological model integrating these visual functions within a moving animal would be invaluable. One important consideration that needs to be made in an integrative model is the interaction among different visuomotor circuits tuned to different visual features. Since these circuits in complex visual environments may activate multiple motor programs simultaneously, circuit mechanisms by which distinct sensorimotor pathways are integrated adaptively are necessary. A foundational theory regarding the interaction of multiple sensorimotor pathways is the theory of EC, which underscores the necessity for a feedback signal that 64 filters out undesired sensory input [23]. Previous behavioral studies argued that such a mechanism may indeed exist in some dipteran species [98, 102]. Recent studies in Drosophila have uncovered the neural correlates of the EC in an array of visual neurons during both spontaneous and visually evoked rapid flight turns [26, 24, 25]. In this study, we present an integrative model of Drosophila visuomotor behaviors that is derived from and validated by behavioral experiments. Results of the experiments provided clear behavioral evidence of an EC in flying Drosophila, which was in line with one type of integration strategy that we used in the model. The model was able to predict the steering behavior of flying Drosophila in response to various visual patterns when they are presented individually as well as in superposition. In this approach, the torque response of an animal, W (), is modeled as a sum of two components: one defined purely by a position response P () and the other by a position-dependent velocity response V () (see Figure 3.1 D). W () = P () + V () 67 (3.1) In this model, the position response can be experimentally obtained if we add torque responses to a visual pattern rotating in the clockwise and counter-clockwise directions, but with respect to the same object position. P () = (Wcw() + Wccw())/2 V () = (Wcw() - Wccw())/2 (3.2) (3.3) where Wcw() denotes the wing response for the clockwise-rotating pattern, and Wccw() for the counterclockwise-rotating pattern. The velocity response, V (), can be obtained similarly, but by a subtraction. To apply the above approach, we tested flies with both clockwise- and counterclockwise-rotating visual patterns (see Figure 3.1 E). Wingbeat signals to the patterns were largely symmetric for the two directions, but with subtle asymmetries, which are likely due to experimental variabilities such as misalignment of the fly's body orientation with respect to the display arena. To minimize the influence of such experimental anomalies, we combined the two L-R WBA signals for a pair of symmetrical patterns after flipping one for its sign as well as the time and used them for the further analyses (see Data Analysis in Methods). When we computed the position functions, P (), for the spot and bar patterns with the above method, we found that they were symmetric with respect to the origin (see Figure 3.1 F). That is, for the rotating bar, the position response was positive when the bar was in the left hemifield, but negative in the right hemifield. This result is consistent with fly's fixation behavior to a vertical bar as this position response would have made flies turn toward the bar in both sides. For the spot pattern, the amplitude of 68 the position function was much smaller than that for the spot, and its overall direction was opposite to that for the bar, which would have made flies turn away from the spot. The velocity function, V (), was nearly zero for the spot, except around the frontal visual field (see Figure 3.1 F), and this is consistent with weak direction dependency in the wing response (see Figure 3.1 E). By contrast, the velocity function for the bar is consistently positive (see Figure 3.1 F), poised to contribute to the flight turn in the direction of the bar movement [64]. The amplitude of the velocity response, however, varied depending on the object position, unlike the nearly constant velocity function estimated in blow flies in response to a moving bar [64]. In response to the moving grating, the velocity response was consistently positive, but its amplitude varied depending on the position (see Figure 3.1 E). To be specific, while tracking a slowly moving bar, for example, flies perform relatively straight flights interspersed with saccadic flight turns [108, 109]. A fly was tethered to a short steel pin fixed at a position by a vertically oriented magnetic field that also allowed it to rotate around its yaw axis with little friction (see Figure 3.3 A). We captured the image of the fly from below in response to visual stimuli and calculated the body angle post hoc (see Figure 3.3 A, Methods). To present the visual patterns at a defined position relative to the fly's heading, we coaxed the fly to be aligned to a reference angle by oscillating a stripe pattern widely across the visual display ("alignment" phase, see Figure 3.3 A bottom). We then presented for 0.5 s the initial frame of the visual pattern ("ready" phase), which is then rotated rapidly for 0.2 seconds in a sigmoidal dynamics ("go" phase) (see Figure 3.3 A). After the movement, the pattern remained static for 2.5 seconds ("freeze" phase). With these experimental results in a magnetically tethered assay, we confirmed that our virtual fly models captured essential dynamics of the visionbased flight control in Drosophila when the patterns are presented individually. In natural conditions, however, multiple patterns may be presented simultaneously in a visual scene. For example when a fly is trying to land on a fruit that is on the foreground and there are objects in the background such as trees, bushes, etc. This led us to further develop the model to add a capacity of controlling their orientation under more complex visual environments. 76 3.3.5 Integrative visuomotor control models in a complex visual environment In natural environments, various visual patterns might simultaneously activate distinct visuomotor circuits. These circuits, if activated, may normally trigger either synergistic or opposing locomotive actions. For instance, when a fly turns to track a foreground object moving against a static background (see Figure 3.4 A), it experiences rotational optic flow from the background in a direction opposite to the flight turn. This optic flow would immediately activate the visual stability reflex that opposes the object-evoked turn. Therefore, this raises the question as to how outputs from different visuomotor circuits integrate to control a shared actuator, such as

Therefore, this raises the question as to how outputs from different visuomotor circuits integrate to control a shared actuator, such as the wing motor system. This problem has been studied in sensory systems of many different animals, typically by analyzing physiological recordings made in behaving conditions [113, 98, 114]. According to the results of these studies, we developed three integrative models. The first model is termed "addition-only model", in which output of the bar and the grating response circuits are added to control the flight orientation (see Figure 3.4 B, see Equation 3.14 in Methods). In the second and third models, an EC is used to set priorities between different visuomotor circuits (see Figure 3.4 C, D). In particular, the EC is derived from the bar-induced motor command and is sent to the grating response system to nullify visual input associated with the bar-evoked turn [113, 98, 114]. In some sensory systems, such motor-related inputs are strong enough to completely silence sensory processing [114], whereas in others the motor-related inputs counteract only undesirable part of the sensory feedback [113, 115].
